title: Words That Sound Alike
description: Try familiar American English sound-alike words, each supported by a direct meaning clue.
cardDescription: Try familiar American English sound-alike words, each supported by a direct meaning clue.
focus: A sound-alike hint points to pronunciation, while the definition identifies the spelling needed in the grid. These clues use common pronunciations and supply the meaning so that the sound is not the only guide.
solvingTip: Read both halves of the clue. A word sounding like another answer still has to match the stated meaning and the crossing letters.
words: Long-eared animal whose name sounds like hair
Medieval armored warrior whose name sounds like night
Ground grain for baking whose name sounds like flower
Culinary herb whose name sounds like time
Iron-based alloy whose name sounds like steal
To put words on paper, sounding like right
Large body of salt water, sounding like see
Male child in a family, sounding like sun
Word for a boy or man, sounding like mail
Simple or undecorated, sounding like plane
Event offering goods at reduced prices, sounding like sail
Animal's rear extension, sounding like tale
To come together with someone, sounding like meat
Opposite of left, sounding like a verb for putting words on paper

answerNotes.HARE: Hare and hair sound alike in common American pronunciation. The animal definition chooses the spelling needed here.
answerNotes.KNIGHT: Knight begins with a silent k. The historical role distinguishes it from night, the dark part of a day.
answerNotes.FLOUR: Flour names the baking ingredient. Flower names a plant's bloom despite the shared pronunciation.
answerNotes.THYME: Thyme is the herb spelling. The silent letters make the sound-alike hint useful alongside the definition.
answerNotes.STEEL: Steel is a material. Steal is a verb with the same common pronunciation but a different spelling and meaning.

title: Words for Groups
description: Find familiar collective words and number groups through people, animals, and everyday objects.
cardDescription: Find familiar collective words and number groups through people, animals, and everyday objects.
focus: Some group words describe a shared activity, while others specify a number or arrangement. The clues keep those categories distinct instead of treating every collection as interchangeable.
solvingTip: Decide whether a clue gives an exact count, an activity, or a physical arrangement. A number word can be more precise than a general collective noun.
words: Organized group of singers performing together
Group working together aboard a boat or on another shared job
Pile of objects arranged one above another
Group of sheep or birds considered together
Group of cattle moving or feeding together
Group cooperating in a game or shared task
Set containing exactly two matching or associated items
Collection of objects gathered or tied into one package
Close grouping of similar things, such as stars or grapes
Large gathering of people in one place

answerNotes.DOZEN: Dozen gives an exact count. A bunch or crowd does not specify one fixed number.
answerNotes.CHOIR: A choir is a singing ensemble. An audience listens, while this group performs.
answerNotes.CREW: Crew describes people with a shared task. Its size depends on the work rather than a fixed count.
answerNotes.TRIO: Trio specifies three. It can describe musicians or another three-member group.
answerNotes.STACK: Stack describes an arrangement. It differs from bundle, where objects are gathered or tied together.

title: Everyday American Spellings
description: Practice common United States spellings through familiar objects and meanings rather than obscure spelling rules.
cardDescription: Practice common United States spellings through familiar objects and meanings rather than obscure spelling rules.
focus: The clues request usual American forms. Some alternatives also appear in American names and publications, so these choices describe common usage rather than declaring every other form incorrect.
solvingTip: Match the meaning first, then use the American spelling requested. Crossings can help with a single or doubled consonant and an omitted letter.
words: Usual American spelling for decorative rings, necklaces, and similar items
Usual American spelling for the middle of something
Common American spelling for a place where plays are performed
Common American spelling for the color between black and white
Usual American spelling for an official permit
Usual American spelling for a hue such as red or blue
Usual American spelling for a person living next door
Usual American spelling for a helpful act done for someone
Usual American spelling for a person making a journey
Usual American spelling for a vehicle wheel's rubber covering
Usual American spelling for an implement that turns soil
Common American spelling for an ordered list of goods
Usual American spelling for the metric unit of length
Usual American spelling for the metric unit of liquid volume

answerNotes.JEWELRY: Jewelry is the common American form. Jewellery is usual in British English.
answerNotes.CENTER: Center is common in American English. Centre may still appear in proper names and in other English varieties.
answerNotes.THEATER: Theater is common in the United States. Theatre also occurs in American names and usage, so it is not universally excluded.
answerNotes.GRAY: Gray is the usual American form. Grey also appears in American proper names and other contexts.
answerNotes.LICENSE: American English uses license as both noun and verb. Some other varieties distinguish the noun licence from the verb license.

title: A Word About Time
description: Match familiar time words with periods, positions in a sequence, and parts of a day.
cardDescription: Match familiar time words with periods, positions in a sequence, and parts of a day.
focus: Some words specify exact units, while others are relative or depend on context. The clues distinguish a fixed ten-year period from broader historical language and from the light around sunrise or sunset.
solvingTip: Ask whether the clue gives a count, a relation to now, or a part of the day. Relative words do not imply a precise number of minutes.
words: Long historical period identified by a distinctive character
Early morning light before and around sunrise
Fading light around the end of evening twilight
Calendar division with a name such as April
One of the year's familiar divisions, such as autumn
Time occurring now rather than before or afterward
Time that has not yet arrived
At a time after the one being considered
Before much more time has passed
Twelve o'clock in the middle of the daytime clock cycle

answerNotes.DECADE: A decade contains ten years. The word alone does not require one particular starting year.
answerNotes.CENTURY: A century contains one hundred years. Numbered historical centuries use a naming convention that differs from casually naming the 1900s.
answerNotes.ERA: Era has no single fixed duration in ordinary historical use. It differs from an exact unit such as a decade.
answerNotes.DAWN: Dawn refers to the beginning of daylight. It is not simply another name for midnight or for the Sun at its highest point.
answerNotes.DUSK: Dusk belongs to the evening transition toward darkness. Exact usage can vary, unlike an exact clock unit.

title: Sounds Around the House
description: Recognize everyday sound words through a door, a clock, an appliance, and a few small household actions.
cardDescription: Recognize everyday sound words through a door, a clock, an appliance, and a few small household actions.
focus: Sound words describe an impression rather than a precisely measured tone. The clues supply a familiar source to separate similar short words and encourage reading the whole description.
solvingTip: Use the source and the character of the sound together. A sustained noise and a single impact usually call for different words.
words: High thin sound from a dry hinge or a small toy
Clear musical ringing from a doorbell or set of bells
Repeated clattering of loose parts in a container
Steady soft spinning sound from a small motor
Continuous rushing sound like escaping air
Short sharp sound when a latch snaps shut
Strained groaning sound of an old floorboard underfoot
Small regular beat made by a traditional clock
Low steady sound from a running refrigerator
Vibrating sound associated with an electric door buzzer
Clear repeated sound of a traditional telephone bell
Dull heavy impact sound of a book landing on a rug
Sound and action of a single water drop falling
Light brief knock made with a fingertip

answerNotes.SQUEAK: Squeak suggests a brief high-pitched sound. Creak often suggests a lower strained sound from moving wood or a hinge.
answerNotes.CHIME: Chime emphasizes a musical ringing quality. It differs from the low impact suggested by thud.
answerNotes.RATTLE: A rattle is a series of small impacts. It can also name a toy designed to make that sound.
answerNotes.WHIR: Whir suggests rapid rotation. It differs from the separate regular beats represented by tick.
answerNotes.HISS: Hiss describes a sustained rushing noise. The clue gives a sound example rather than instructions to inspect an appliance.
